newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper to back extradition - radio.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper to back extradition - radio.

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper will issue a statement in New York on Monday expressing tentative support for efforts to lift his country's ban on the extradition of drug lords, Colombian radio said.
The Caracol radio network said the statement would be issued shortly after Samper's speech to the United Nations General Assembly, scheduled for 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT).
"Colombia accepts the usefulness of multilateral extradition," the statement says in part, according to Caracol.

It stresses, however, that the government would back moves to lift Colombia's constitutional ban on extradition only after the Colombian Congress approved legislation Samper submitted in mid-July to stiffen prison sentences for drug trafficking and permit the confiscation of drug barons' property.

The statement would mark the government's first official reaction to legislation proposed by a ruling Liberal Party lawmaker earlier this month calling for the immediate reinstitution of extradition in Colombia.

The legislation proposed by Luis Guillermo Giraldo, a leading Samper critic, was not expected to win approval without the president's personal backing. And even with Samper's approval, it could be scuttled by broad opposition, reflected in recent polls showing that an overwhelming majority of Colombians oppose extradition.
Colombia's Congress clamped a ban on extradition in 1991, infuriating U.S. drug experts, who argue that detention in secure prisons in the United States is what Colombian traffickers fear the most.

The ban was passed after hundreds of people, including three presidential candidates, a justice minister, high court judges, journalists and scores of police officers were killed in a campaign of assassinations and bombings that drug lords waged against extradition in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno formally requested the extradition in June of brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, the billionaire leaders of the Cali drug cartel.
But the government denied the request, arguing that a 1979 U.S.-Colombian extradition treaty had been invalidated by the constitutional ban.

It was not immediately clear if Samper would back calls to reactivate the treaty retroactively, allowing for extradition of the Rodriguez Orejuelas and other drug kingpins wanted in the United States.
Colombia, the world's leading exporter of cocaine and a top supplier of heroin to the United States, is under heavy U.S. pressure to step up its war on criminal drug syndicates.

Samper, whose 1994 election campaign allegedly received millions of dollars in financing from the Cali cartel, has insisted repeatedly that Colombians are more victims of the drug trade than its villians.
